title: Paper clay sun face relief panel
subtitle: A 20 cm wall-mounted sun face in air-dry paper clay with sculpted rays
excerpt: A sun face relief panel is a circular wall piece about 20 cm across, built in air-dry paper clay with a sculpted central face and radiating rays pressed and formed around it. Paper clay is air-dry clay reinforced with paper fibre, which makes it stronger and less prone to cracking than standard air-dry clay. Intermediate makers building their first relief sculpture find the paper fibre forgiving when adding thin ray details.
sourceNotes: Sun face relief panel design derived from first principles. Historical sun face imagery referenced from V&A open-access collection (English and Continental decorative arts). Paper clay properties referenced from standard ceramics literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dry clay blended with paper fibre for added strength and crack resistance; needs no kiln
Sculpture in which forms project forward from a flat background, rather than being fully three-dimensional

Fully air-dried and unfired; pale, lightweight, and fragile until sealed

content.text: A sun face relief panel is a circular wall piece about 20 cm across, built in air-dry
paper clay

with a sculpted face at the centre and radiating rays around the circumference. No kiln is needed: the finished panel dries in air and mounts on a wall with a recessed hanging loop pressed in before drying. An intermediate maker building their first figurative
relief
piece will find the paper fibre reduces cracking in the thin ray tips.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay, thinned with water)
Acrylic paint, gold or ochre base coat
Acrylic paint, raw umber or dark brown for shading

content.text: Preparation

Sketch the design on paper before cutting clay. Draw a circle 20 cm across. Inside it, mark the face area as a circle about 10 cm across at the centre. Sketch 12-16 rays of varied lengths radiating from the edge of the face circle to the outer edge of the panel. Note which rays will be pointed, which rounded, and where any additional small detail rays will sit between the main rays. Cut out the paper sketch to use as a template for the base slab.
Building the panel

Roll a slab of paper clay 8 mm thick. Use guide strips of equal thickness on each side to keep the rolling pin level. The slab needs to be at least 22 cm across to allow for slight shrinkage and trimming.

Lay your paper template over the slab. Cut around the circle with the fettling knife, holding it vertical to keep the edge clean. Lift the circle to a flat board or tile where it will dry undisturbed.

Press a hanging loop into the back of the base slab now, before adding any surface relief. Roll a clay rope 8 mm thick and 5 cm long. Bend it into a D shape and score-and-slip both ends onto the back of the slab in the upper third of the circle. The loop sits flat against the back and should project about 1.5 cm clear of the surface to accept a nail or hook.

Roll clay for the rays: small tapered ovals about 4-6 mm thick at the base and tapering to 2 mm at the tip. Make the ray shapes individually, using the sketch as a guide for length and width. Longer rays can be 6-8 cm; shorter filler rays 3-4 cm.

Score and slip the base of each ray and the corresponding area on the base circle. Position all rays before pressing any down firmly, so you can adjust spacing. When the arrangement is satisfying, press each ray base firmly onto the slab, blending the clay at the join with a damp wooden rib.

Build the face features next. Roll a small ball of clay about 5 cm across for the central raised face area. Press it gently into the centre of the base circle and smooth the edges down onto the slab with a wooden rib, creating a gentle dome with a 10 cm footprint.

Shape the eyes as two leaf-shaped pads of clay, each about 2.5 cm long and 1 cm wide at the centre, with upturned outer corners. Score and slip in place. Press small rope eyebrows above them. Roll two small almond shapes for closed eyelids or use the needle tool to incise open irises.

Form the nose as a triangular wedge about 1.5 cm tall. Score and slip onto the face centre. For cheeks, press two small flattened balls of clay either side of the nose and blend the edges down smoothly with a damp sponge.

Shape the mouth as a curved rope of clay about 3 cm long, pressed and blended into a smile. Add a thin rope of clay above it to form the upper lip definition. Use the needle tool to add a centre line between the lips if desired.

Use the wooden rib and needle tool to refine all the relief elements while the clay is still soft. Smooth transitions between the raised features and the base slab. Check the panel from the side: the highest points (nose, central dome) should project no more than 12-15 mm from the base slab to keep the piece stable during drying.
Drying
Cover the panel loosely with a sheet of plastic and leave it to reach
leather-hard
over 24 hours. At leather-hard, refine any rough areas gently with a damp sponge. Do not press hard: the relief elements are not yet fully bonded throughout. Remove the cover and allow to dry to
bone-dry

over a further three to five days. Drying in a warm room speeds the process but increases crack risk in the thin ray tips; a cool steady environment is safer. Bone-dry paper clay is pale throughout, not just on the surface, and no longer cold to the touch.
Finishing

Apply a base coat of gold or ochre acrylic paint over the entire front and edges using the mop brush. Allow to dry fully. Mix a small amount of raw umber with water to a very thin wash and brush over the whole surface. Immediately wipe back the high points with a damp cloth, leaving the darker wash sitting in the recessed areas and joins. This dry-brush shading gives the piece depth. Seal with two coats of matte varnish, allowing each coat to dry between applications.
Care

Hang in a dry indoor location. Do not hang in a bathroom or kitchen where steam is regular. Dust with a dry soft brush. The hanging loop is load-rated for the weight of the panel only; do not attach additional items to it.
Variations

Make a moon face companion piece using the same base circle but with crescent ray shapes and a waxing-moon cheek cutout. Paint in silver and blue-grey tones. The two pieces work as a pair on either side of a door or window.

Press leaf-vein texture into each ray before they are joined to the base, using the back of a real leaf or the needle tool. The texture catches the shading wash and adds complexity without requiring extra modelling skill.
Scale up to a 30 cm panel for a statement piece. Use a thicker base slab at 10 mm and add a second hanging loop in the lower third of the back to prevent the panel from swinging forward on the wall.
Troubleshooter

items.cause: The tips dried faster than the thick base slab, creating tension cracks at the thinnest points
items.fix: Keep the panel covered with plastic for the first 48 hours to slow and even out drying. If a crack appears at leather-hard, dampen the area, press the crack closed, and smooth with a damp tool

items.problem: Ray separates from the base slab
items.cause: The score-and-slip join was not pressed firmly enough, or the clay surfaces were too dry when joined
items.fix: Dampen both surfaces, apply fresh slip, re-press the ray, and smooth the join. Support the ray with a small rolled clay prop while the repair firms

items.problem: Face features look flat and cartoonish
items.cause: Features were applied as flat pads rather than built with gradual thickness variation
items.fix: At leather-hard, use a needle tool to under-cut slightly beneath the lower lip and the lower eyelid edges. The shadow line this creates adds the illusion of depth

items.cause: The base slab was rolled unevenly, creating a thick area that dried at a different rate
items.fix: At leather-hard, place the panel face-up on a flat board and weight the edges gently with small tiles for 12 hours. Once bone-dry, warping cannot be corrected
